activity_context.topic_title: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals

examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals Over Parametric Curves
examples.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy^2+ 2xz.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $\mathbf r(t)= \langle e^{t}, t, e^{-t}\rangle$ for $t\in \left[0,1\right],$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{C} \nabla f\cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r.$
examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0,1⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨e,1,\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0,1)$ and $\left(e, 1, \dfrac{1}{e}\right).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e,1,\frac{1}{e})-f(1,0,1) \\  & =(e(1)^{2}+2\cdot e\cdot \frac{1}{e})-(1(0)^{2}+2(1)(1)) \\  & =(e+2)-2 \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$
